cards.title: Non-clashing teaching dimension versus VC dimension
cards.formal: For every finite set X and every nonempty concept class C⊆2ˣ, is NCTD(C)≤VC(C)? Equivalently, if C has VC dimension d, does there exist a teaching map assigning at most d correctly labeled examples to each concept such that no two distinct concepts are mutually consistent with one another’s assigned examples? Both positive and negative examples are allowed. The target constant is exactly one, not merely a bound O(d).
cards.why: Would show that every finite concept class can be taught with at most its VC dimension many examples per concept in the non-clashing model, giving a sharp link between learning capacity and teaching complexity.
cards.status_note: Read the finite-domain no-clash definition and conclusion, the expanded JMLR treatment, and the COLT 2024 special-case results. Later searches through 12 September 2026 also found work on computing positive graph-ball teaching maps, but no proof or counterexample to the universal signed NCTD≤VC inequality. Search is not exhaustive.

cards.definitions: A concept C∈C is a subset of the finite instance set X, identified with its indicator function 1_C:X→{0,1}. A labeled sample is an unordered subset of X×{0,1}. It is consistent with C if each (x,y) in it has y=1_C(x). A teaching map T assigns a sample T(C) consistent with C to every concept C in the class. It is non-clashing if, for every distinct C,D∈C, T(C) is not consistent with D or T(D) is not consistent with C. Equivalently, some point appearing in either teaching set has different labels under C and D. The condition is pairwise: T(C) need not by itself distinguish C from every other concept. A positive example has label 1 and a negative example has label 0; both count as one example. The size of T is max_{C∈C}|T(C)|, and NCTD(C) is the minimum of that size over all non-clashing teaching maps. The minimum exists because X and C are finite and giving all labels is a valid map. No sample order, extra message or additional side information is part of this definition. A subset S⊆X is shattered by C when {C∩S:C∈C}=2ˢ. The VC dimension VC(C) is the maximum cardinality of a shattered set. For a singleton concept class it is zero, and the empty teaching set works. The statement quantifies over all finite X and nonempty C, including that case; it concerns existence of a map, without an efficiency or encoding-size requirement on constructing it. The positive-only parameter NCTD⁺ restricts T(C) to samples with label 1 and can be larger. It is not the parameter in this conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the exact inequality for every finite concept class by establishing existence of a valid map of maximum size at most its VC dimension, or give a finite concept class and a proof that every non-clashing teaching map has larger maximum size. A quadratic bound or even a larger-constant linear bound is insufficient. A separation for positive-only maps, another teaching model, or an algorithmic hardness result for finding maps does not refute this existence statement.

context_blocks.title: Known general bounds leave a substantial gap
context_blocks.text: The source and journal article give a universal upper bound quadratic in VC dimension. Their conclusion asks for the sharper inequality with coefficient one, and reports no counterexample to that inequality.

context_blocks.title: Finite maximum classes satisfy the target
context_blocks.text: If a class of VC dimension d on X attains Sauer’s size bound Σ_{i=0}^d binomial(|X|,i), the cited representation-map result supplies a non-clashing map of size d. Maximum classes are a special case, not all finite classes.

context_blocks.title: Graph-ball results provide further special cases
context_blocks.text: The COLT 2024 paper constructs small maps for balls in particular graph classes and explicitly repeats the general open question. A size-four upper bound together with a VC-dimension-three upper bound for another family does not prove NCTD exceeds VC there.

context_blocks.title: The teaching convention matters
context_blocks.text: The journal article separately studies stronger restrictions on avoiding collusion. Their optimal teaching parameter need not equal NCTD. Likewise, a map for the concepts themselves is not automatically a sample-compression scheme that must reconstruct from arbitrary samples.

cards.context:
The source and journal article give a universal upper bound quadratic in VC dimension. Their conclusion asks for the sharper inequality with coefficient one, and reports no counterexample to that inequality.

If a class of VC dimension d on X attains Sauer’s size bound Σ_{i=0}^d binomial(|X|,i), the cited representation-map result supplies a non-clashing map of size d. Maximum classes are a special case, not all finite classes.

The COLT 2024 paper constructs small maps for balls in particular graph classes and explicitly repeats the general open question. A size-four upper bound together with a VC-dimension-three upper bound for another family does not prove NCTD exceeds VC there.

The journal article separately studies stronger restrictions on avoiding collusion. Their optimal teaching parameter need not equal NCTD. Likewise, a map for the concepts themselves is not automatically a sample-compression scheme that must reconstruct from arbitrary samples.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
